Mary never undertook to write to Bath; the whole labour of sustaining a tardy and unsatisfactory correspondence with Elizabeth was left to Anne.

They had finished breakfast only a short while before Captain and Mrs. Harville arrived with Captain Benwick, according to their arrangement for a final walk about Lyme. By one they ought to be departing for Uppercross; until then they intended to remain together, and in the open air for as much of the time as possible.

Scarcely had the whole party reached the street when Anne perceived Captain Benwick drawing near her. Their conversation of the previous evening had certainly not discouraged him from seeking her again. For a while they walked together, speaking once more of Mr. Scott and Lord Byron, and finding themselves as little able as before—or as any other pair of readers—to agree precisely upon the excellence of either. Then some occurrence produced a nearly general rearrangement of the company, and Captain Harville took Captain Benwick's place beside her.

“Miss Elliot,” he said in a somewhat lowered voice, “you have done a kindness in persuading that poor fellow to talk so freely. I wish he might enjoy such company more frequently. I know that being so confined is harmful to him; but what are we to do? We cannot separate.”

“No,” replied Anne, “I can readily believe that impossible. Yet perhaps with time—we know what time accomplishes in every sorrow. You must remember, Captain Harville, that your friend's mourning may still be called recent. It was only last summer, I understand.”

“Yes, indeed,” he answered, sighing deeply, “only June.”

“And perhaps he did not hear of it immediately.”

“Not before the first week in August, when he returned from the Cape, newly appointed to the Grappler. I was in Plymouth, afraid to hear of his arrival. He sent letters in, but the Grappler had orders for Portsmouth. The news must reach him there; but who would deliver it? Not I. I would as willingly have been strung up at the yardarm. No one could manage it but that excellent fellow”—indicating Captain Wentworth. “The Laconia had reached Plymouth a week earlier, and was in no danger of being sent out again. For everything else he took his chance. He applied for leave, but, never waiting for the answer, journeyed day and night to Portsmouth, rowed straight out to the Grappler, and remained beside the poor fellow a whole week. That is what he did; no other man could have saved poor James. You may judge, Miss Elliot, how dear he is to us!”

Anne judged with complete conviction, and answered as fully as her feelings permitted, or as his appeared capable of enduring. He was too deeply moved to return to the subject; when next he spoke, it concerned something altogether different.

Ten minutes afterwards, his face white with fear and his eyes distraught with sorrow, Lord Arthur Savile hurried out of Bentinck House. He forced a passage through the fur-clad footmen gathered about the great striped awning, apparently neither seeing nor hearing anything. The night was bitterly cold, and the gaslights around the square flickered and blazed in the sharp wind; yet his hands were feverishly hot, and his brow seemed on fire. He pressed onward and onward with something of a drunken man's step. A policeman watched him curiously as he went past, and a beggar who shuffled out from an archway seeking charity drew back in alarm at the sight of misery exceeding his own. Once he paused beneath a lamp to inspect his hands. Already he fancied he could distinguish bloodstains on them, and a weak cry escaped his shaking lips.

Murder! That was what the palm-reader had discovered there. Murder! The night itself appeared aware of it, and the mournful wind seemed to shriek the word into his ear. It filled the shadowy street corners. It leered down from the house roofs.

He reached the Park first, drawn, it seemed, by its gloomy woods. Wearily he rested against the railings, pressing his forehead to the cool, wet iron and attending to the quivering silence among the trees. “Murder! Murder!” he murmured again and again, as though repetition might lessen the word's horror. His own voice sent a shudder through him, yet he almost wished that Echo would overhear and rouse the sleeping city from its dreams. A frantic impulse seized him to detain some passing stranger and confess it all.

Afterwards he strayed across Oxford Street and into narrow, disreputable lanes. Two painted women jeered as he passed. From a black courtyard sounded curses and blows, succeeded by piercing cries; on a wet doorstep he noticed the bent shapes of old age and poverty huddled together. An unfamiliar compassion possessed him. Had these offspring of misery and sin been destined for their fate, as he was for his? Were they also nothing but puppets in some monstrous spectacle?

Yet what impressed him was less suffering's mystery than its comedy: its utter futility and grotesque absence of purpose. Everything appeared so disconnected, so devoid of harmony! He marvelled at the clash between the day's facile optimism and the actual conditions of existence. He was still exceedingly young.

Presently he discovered that he stood before Marylebone Church. The quiet road resembled a long ribbon of burnished silver, marked here and there with the dark arabesques of moving shadows.

It's curious, but everyone who disappears is supposedly spotted in San Francisco. It must be a delightful city, with all the attractions of the next world.”

“What do you think has happened to Basil?” asked Dorian, lifting his Burgundy toward the light and wondering how he could talk about the subject so calmly.

“I haven't the faintest idea. If Basil wants to hide, that's none of my business. If he's dead, I would rather not think of him. Death is the one thing that ever frightens me. I hate it.”

“Why?” the younger man asked tiredly.

“Because,” said Lord Henry, passing the gold lattice of an open scent box beneath his nose, “these days you can survive everything else. Death and vulgarity are the only two facts of the nineteenth century that we cannot explain away. Let's take our coffee in the music room, Dorian. You must play some Chopin for me. The man my wife ran away with played Chopin beautifully. Poor Victoria! I was very fond of her. The house feels rather lonely without her. Of course, marriage is simply a habit, and a bad one. Still, we miss even our worst habits when we lose them. Perhaps those are the ones we miss most. They form such an essential part of our personalities.”

Without answering, Dorian got up from the table and went into the next room. He sat at the piano, letting his fingers wander over the black and white ivory keys. Once the coffee arrived, he stopped playing and looked across at Lord Henry. “Harry, has it ever occurred to you that Basil might have been murdered?”

Lord Henry yawned. “Basil was well liked, and he always wore a Waterbury watch. Why would anyone murder him? He wasn't clever enough to make enemies. Naturally, he had an extraordinary gift for painting. But a man can paint like Velasquez and still be perfectly dull. Basil really was rather dull. He interested me only once: years ago, when he told me he adored you passionately and you were the central inspiration for his art.”

“I was very fond of Basil,” Dorian said, with sadness in his voice. “But aren't people saying he was murdered?”

“Oh, some newspapers say so. It doesn't strike me as at all likely. I know there are dreadful places in Paris, but Basil wasn't the kind of man who would visit them. He had no curiosity. That was his greatest failing.”

“What would you say, Harry, if I told you that I murdered Basil?” asked the younger man.
